analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from getting or using workers' genetic information without written consent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred on July 22, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for employers to obtain, share, or use genetic information about workers or job applicants unless the worker signed a separate written authorization and was told what the employer planned to do with it. Workers whose genetic information was taken or used improperly could sue for actual damages. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants, who would gain control over whether employers can access their genetic test results and family medical history, and the ability to sue if employers misuse that information.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from obtaining genetic information about an employee or job applicant unless the person signs a written, stand-alone authorization naming the employer [S2][S3].
Requires employers who want genetic information to first give the worker a written statement of how they intend to use it [S2][S3].
Lets employees or applicants sue for actual damages and equitable relief if an employer obtains, discloses, or uses genetic information without valid authorization [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face new consent and paperwork requirements before accessing genetic information and potential damages liability for misuse.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on a consent framework, meaning workers could still be pressured to sign authorizations to get or keep a job, which later legislation addressed by banning use of genetic information in employment decisions outright.
It creates new compliance and paperwork obligations for employers of all sizes, which business groups generally opposed as burdensome in this era of genetic-privacy proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are meaningful but weaker than what later became law: because the bill is consent-based, an employer can still collect genetic information if the worker signs, and workers may feel they have no real choice. It would nonetheless give workers a clear right to know and a way to sue. The cost to employers is modest compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to committee the day it was introduced, a subcommittee took it in September 1997, and neither acted again before Congress ended in January 1999, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II introduced the bill on July 22, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On September 19, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed.
No further action was taken in the 105th Congress, which ended January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who gather or use genetic information about workers kept the ability to do so without the consent and notice rules this bill would have imposed. Twelve years later, Congress passed GINA, which restricts employers' use of genetic information more strictly than this bill did.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, until GINA later became law

for.name: Joseph P. Kennedy II
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee; no markup, hearing, or floor action followed its referral.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in September 1997 and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote or hearing ever occurred, so the partisan split on this bill never took shape; both the sponsor and its sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican action is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required written, stand-alone consent and advance disclosure before an employer could obtain genetic information, plus damages liability for misuse. Employer groups opposed such genetic-privacy mandates as compliance burdens in this era.

industries.industry: Genetic testing and medical records industries
industries.note: Any pathway for employers to request or receive genetic tests or records would have narrowed, since employers could no longer obtain genetic information without the worker's explicit authorization.
